Here's where your argument falls apart: contrary to popular belief, oil does not come from "dinosaurs". Oil was formed largely by a mass extinction event that caused an unimaginable amount of ocean plant life(mostly made of carbon) to die. The reason this is important is that those plants trapped an insane amount of carbon deep in the Earth(much much more than dinosaurs would have). The lack of extra carbon created a climate system(if we consider our atmosphere a more or less closed system) that modern mammals evolved in. Yes, it's not the way the planet has always been and, yes, the Earth's climate isn't stable on a regional basis, BUT the content of the atmosphere has been more or less stable for hundreds of millions of years. The chemical composition of the atmosphere will alter how well it retains heat and myriad of other properties. Changing the content of the atmosphere therefore has a dramatic effect on climate. Considering the fact that Homo sapiens sapiens only evolved in the last few hundred thousand years, I'd consider an increase in total carbon to levels that haven't been seen for hundreds of millions of years pretty damn significant. In fact, I can't even comprehend how a person could argue that literally changing the composition of an atmosphere won't change its properties.

Every time we think we have figured out something we observe an event that doesn't fit with what we thought. We're seeing this in just about every field of serious study; it's what makes studying nature so awesome. So, everything you're writing with such certainty may change completely tomorrow with some new observation. We know the Earth has not warmed in the way the models said it would, we know the Earth seems to regulate it's temperatures through the hydrologic cycle, we learned a few years ago that the outgassing of CO2 from our atmosphere is greater than what we thought, so that was incorrectly modeled, we've seen that global temperatures did not change as the models predicted and that this may, at least in part, be because the models did not account for the impact of decreased solar activity which seems to match the level of solar activity recorded during the Little Ice Age, we've also seen that much of the change in ice cover in the Antarctic seems to be in reaction to volcanic activity, and that even with that activity the change was not as significant as the models predicted, we've also seen that Arctic ice actually increased in 2014 despite the models' predictions. As long as observations continue to be not just different, but in many cases be opposite from what the models predict, the prudent, the reasonable thing to do is to remain skeptical and to oppose any political force that seeks to change our lives.
